question: How have Apple's regulatory disclosures changed from 2023 through 2025, and what actions does management describe?

notes: Years are read as each company’s own fiscal years.

scopes.description: AAPL: fiscal years FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 (FY2023, FY2024, FY2025).

brief.title: Apple Regulatory Disclosure Evolution: FY2023–FY2025
brief.executiveSummary: Apple's regulatory risk disclosures have grown materially more specific and consequential from FY2023 through FY2025, moving from forward-looking DMA compliance obligations to reporting concrete actions already taken—including EU App Store restructuring, U.S. court-ordered commission restrictions, and a new Google antitrust ruling with direct revenue implications. Management describes an expanding set of implemented changes (alternative distribution, fee structures, payment processing) alongside ongoing challenges from the European Commission and U.S. antitrust litigation. By FY2025, the disclosure landscape also incorporates new macro-regulatory risks—tariffs on imports from multiple countries and AI/machine learning legal considerations—that were absent in FY2023.
followUpQuestions: What specific financial liabilities or accruals has Apple recorded in its FY2024 and FY2025 financial statements in connection with App Store litigation and DMA-related proceedings?
How does Apple's FY2025 10-K describe the quantitative contribution of search licensing revenue to its Services segment, and what contingency disclosures accompany the Google antitrust remedy risk?
What changes, if any, did Apple disclose in its FY2025 quarterly filings (10-Qs) regarding the status of the European Commission's challenge to its DMA compliance plan?

How have Apple's disclosures regarding data privacy obligations—particularly for health, biometric and financial data—evolved across FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 in light of the AI/machine learning risk language added in FY2025?

keyFindings.title: DMA Compliance: From Obligation to Implemented Changes
keyFindings.finding: In FY2023, Apple disclosed it was required to comply with the EU Digital Markets Act by March 2024 and described future changes as anticipated. By FY2024, Apple reported it had already implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari in the EU, including new business terms, alternative fee structures, alternative distribution methods, alternative payment processing, and additional developer tools and APIs. FY2025 disclosures repeat these implemented changes and add that the compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission and may be challenged further by private litigants.

FY2023 and FY2024 disclosures described U.S. App Store changes to developer-consumer communications regarding alternative purchasing mechanisms as implemented actions. FY2025 adds a materially new element: Apple is 'currently subject to a court order preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make,' a specific legal constraint not present in prior-year filings.
keyFindings.title: U.S. App Store: Court Order Restricting Commissions Added in FY2025
Google Antitrust Ruling Introduces Direct Revenue Risk in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 and FY2024 filings disclosed that Apple's search licensing arrangements with Google and others were subject to government investigations and legal proceedings. FY2025 adds that on August 5, 2024, Google was found to have violated U.S. antitrust laws, and on September 2, 2025, the D.C. District Court ordered certain remedies. The filing warns that if DOJ-proposed remedies—such as prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution—were implemented, they 'could materially adversely affect the Company's ability to earn revenue from such licensing arrangements.'

keyFindings.title: U.S. Antitrust Litigation Named Explicitly from FY2024 Onward
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 disclosures referenced antitrust investigations in various jurisdictions generally. FY2024 and FY2025 filings specifically name civil antitrust lawsuits in the U.S. alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for 'performance smartphones' and 'smartphones' generally in violation of U.S. antitrust laws, representing a more granular and escalated disclosure.

keyFindings.title: New Risk Categories Emerge in FY2025: Tariffs and AI
keyFindings.finding: FY2025 introduces two regulatory risk categories absent from FY2023 and FY2024 filings. First, beginning in the second quarter of FY2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, the EU and others, with a Section 232 semiconductor investigation also noted. Second, AI and machine learning are cited as exacerbating patent and data privacy risks, including risks of novel IP claims and inadvertent personal data disclosure.

keyFindings.title: ESG and Social Disclosure Language Shifts in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 and FY2024 filings framed ESG risk around stakeholder expectations and reporting obligations, referencing climate change, human and civil rights, and diversity, equity and inclusion. FY2025 reframes this section under 'Varied stakeholder expectations about social and other issues,' removing explicit ESG terminology and referencing 'evolving, varied and at times conflicting federal, state and international laws, executive orders, regulations and standards,' reflecting a more legally cautious and politically neutral framing.

investmentConsiderations.text: The FY2025 court order barring Apple from imposing commissions or fees on certain purchases, combined with the DMA's alternative fee structures and distribution requirements already in place in the EU, represents a compounding structural pressure on App Store economics. Diligence teams should assess the cumulative revenue and margin impact of these constraints, noting that the filings warn such changes could reduce App Store sales and commission rates.

The Google antitrust ruling and associated court remedies introduce a specific, named revenue risk to Apple's search licensing income. The FY2025 filing explicitly warns that DOJ-proposed remedies prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial search distribution terms 'could materially adversely affect the Company's ability to earn revenue from such licensing arrangements,' a risk that was only generically described in FY2023 and FY2024.

The FY2025 tariff disclosure—covering imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, plus a Section 232 semiconductor investigation—signals a new and material supply chain and cost risk not present in prior filings. The filing notes the ultimate impact 'remains uncertain' and depends on further government actions, making this a key area for scenario analysis in any financial model.

The progressive escalation from anticipated DMA compliance (FY2023) to implemented changes under Commission challenge (FY2025) suggests ongoing regulatory execution risk in the EU. The filing notes the DMA 'provides for significant fines and penalties for noncompliance' and that 'many risks will remain' even after Apple's implemented changes, indicating that EU regulatory exposure is not resolved.

evidenceGaps: No 10-Q filings are included in the excerpts; intra-year regulatory developments between annual filings (e.g., Q1–Q3 FY2025 or FY2024) are not covered.

The filings do not quantify the revenue contribution from Google search licensing arrangements, so the financial magnitude of the Google antitrust remedy risk cannot be assessed from these excerpts alone.
The filings do not disclose the specific fine amounts or financial penalties Apple has incurred or accrued in connection with DMA non-compliance proceedings.
The financial impact of the U.S. court order restricting App Store commissions is not quantified in the excerpts.
The excerpts do not cover any FY2025 10-Q filings that might contain more recent updates on the Google remedy proceedings or DMA Commission actions after the FY2025 10-K filing date.

Item 7.    Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of OperationsThe following discussion should be read in conjunction with the consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes included in Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K. This Item generally discusses 2025 and 2024 items and year-to-year comparisons between 2025 and 2024. Discussions of 2023 items and year-to-year comparisons between 2024 and 2023 are not included, and can be found in “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” in Part II, Item 7 of the Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended September 28, 2024.Product, Service and Software AnnouncementsThe Company announces new product, service and software offerings at various times during the year. Significant announcements during fiscal year 2025 included the following:First Quarter 2025:•MacBook Pro•Mac mini•iMac•iPad miniSecond Quarter 2025:•iPhone 16e•iPad Air•iPad•MacBook Air•Mac StudioThird Quarter 2025:•iOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26, iPadOS 26, watchOS 26, visionOS 26 and tvOS 26Fourth Quarter 2025:•iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max•Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3 and Apple Watch Ultra 3•AirPods Pro 3Fiscal PeriodThe Company’s fiscal year is the 52- or 53-week period that ends on the last Saturday of September. An additional week is included in the first fiscal quarter every five or six years to realign the Company’s fiscal quarters with calendar quarters, which occurred in the first quarter of 2023. The Company’s fiscal years 2025 and 2024 spanned 52 weeks each, whereas fiscal year 2023 spanned 53 weeks.Macroeconomic ConditionsMacroeconomic conditions, including inflation, interest rates and currency fluctuations, have directly and indirectly impacted, and could in the future materially impact, the Company’s results of operations and financial condition.Apple Inc. | 2025 Form 10-K | 21Tariffs and Other MeasuresBeginning in the second quarter of 2025, new U.S. Tariffs were announced, including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, among others. In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, reciprocal tariffs on imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures. Various modifications to the U.S. Tariffs have been announced and further changes could be made in the future, which may include additional sector-based tariffs or other measures. For example, the U.S. Department of Commerce has initiated an investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, into, among other things, imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including downstream products that contain semiconductors. Tariffs and other measures that are applied to the Company’s products or their components can have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition, including impacting the Company’s supply chain, the availability of rare earths and other raw materials and components, pricing and gross margin. The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether additional or incremental U.S. Tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall magnitude and duration of these measures.

citations.text: Compliance with these laws and regulations is onerous and expensive. New and changing laws and regulations can adversely affect the Company’s business by increasing the Company’s costs, limiting the Company’s ability to offer a product, service or feature to customers, imposing changes to the design of the Company’s products and services, impacting customer demand for the Company’s products and services, and requiring changes to the Company’s supply chain and its business. New and changing laws and regulations can also create uncertainty about how such laws and regulations will be interpreted and applied. These risks and costs may increase as the Company’s products and services are introduced into specialized applications, including health and financial services. The Company has implemented policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations, but there can be no assurance the Company’s employees, contractors or agents will not violate such laws and regulations or the Company’s policies and procedures. If the Company is found to have violated laws and regulations, it could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition. Regulatory changes and other actions that materially adversely affect the Company’s business may be announced with little or no advance notice and the Company may not be able to effectively mitigate all adverse impacts from such measures. For example, the Company is subject to changing regulations relating to the export and import of its products. Although the Company has programs, policies and procedures in place that are designed to satisfy regulatory requirements, there can be no assurance that such policies and procedures will be effective in preventing a violation or a claim of a violation. In addition, some stakeholders may disagree with the Company’s goals and initiatives.
